arguments.issue_text: Evidentiary value of the handwriting expert's report regarding the authorship of the suicide letter.
appellant_arguments: The expert report, even if admissible, cannot be the sole basis to conclude the authorship of the suicide letter; the court must look at all evidence to see if proven facts and circumstances support the conclusion.

The Trial Court should have conducted its own comparison of the handwriting on the suicide letter and considered all circumstances to determine if the letter was indeed written by the alleged author and no one else.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a conviction to be sustained on the strength of circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn must be fully established. These circumstances must be of a definite tendency unerringly pointing towards the guilt of theaccused, and when taken cumulatively, they should form a complete chain that leaves no escape from the conclusion that the crime was committed by the accused. The circumstances must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt and must exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved. The standard of proof requires that the circumstances 'must be' established, not merely 'may be' established.
obiter: While it is not impermissible to base a finding regarding the authorship of a document solely on the opinion of a handwriting expert, it is a rule of prudence not to do so due to the imperfect nature of the science.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution has failed to prove a chain of incriminating circumstances sufficient to conclusively point out that in all human probability it was the two accused, or any one of them, and no one else, who had committed the murder. The court's examination of the enumerated circumstances led to the conclusion that they did not, individually or cumulatively, unerringly point towards the guilt of the accused and rule out all other hypotheses.
legal_tests_applied: For a conviction to be sustained on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met: (i) the circumstances relied upon by the prosecution must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; (ii) those circumstances must have a definite tendency unerringly pointing towards the guilt of the accused; (iii) the circumstances, taken cumulatively, must form a chain so complete that there is no escape from the conclusion that within all human probability the crime was committed by the accused; (iv) the circumstances must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused being guilty; and (v) they must exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.
policy_considerations: The court must adopt a 'most cautious approach' when the evidence adduced by the prosecution is open to suspicion, particularly if it appears that the police may have deliberately attributed similar confessional statements to different accused persons in order to create evidence against all of them.
